new_statements.quote: 4.1. Length and tone. Length and tone are not considered to be pertinent on the phonemic word level. 4.2. Stress. Stress is predictable and therefore non-phonemic. The following rules of stress placement apply to the majority of words: 1. Stress is ultimate if the final syllable of the word is closed. /mařawaY/ (ma.řa'waY) 'beard' /wunini?/ (wu.ni'ni?) 'centepede' /lunam/ (lu'nam) 'tree root' /hawhi?/ (haw'hi?) 'a moss' 2. Stress is penultimate if the final syllable of the word is open. /blohe/ ('blo.hɛ) 'loose' /Wate/ ('Wa.tɛ) 'mountain' /tumwage/ (tu'mwa.ŋgɛ) 'post' /niYene/ (nɩ'Yɛ.nɛ) 'skin irritation'

I read the page images directly (ocr_baker1981/ = printed p.31, i-03/i-04 = pp.2-3, q-35 = p.34, p-01 = title page) rather than relying on the noisy tesseract text. Printed p.31 reads exactly: '4. The following rules of stress placement apply to the majority of words: 1. Stress is ultimate if the final syllable of the word is closed. /mařawaY/ (ma.řa'waY) 'beard' /wunini?/ (wu.ni'ni?) 'centepede' /…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and computed at the right edge: it falls on the final syllable when that syllable is closed (ends in a consonant, glottal stop included) and on the penultimate syllable when the final syllable is open; i.e. a final heavy (CVC) syllable attracts stress, otherwise penult. Stated to hold for 'the majority of words'.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge that the rules 'apply to the majority of words'; no exceptional items listed, and sec. 7 'Unresolved issues' (pp. 47-48) raises nothing about stress. Sec. 0.2 (p. 3): 'Since stress is predictable, it is not usually written.'
new_statements.domain_note: Phonemic word, citation forms (c. 1,000-word corpus); examples are mono-morphemic nouns/adjectives. Intonation treated separately (sec. 4.3). Data from Tumam village, central dialect (Urat II / Yehre), collected 1979-1980.
new_statements.identity_note: Baker & Baker 1981 describe the central dialect, 'Urat II', from Tumam village (the Yehre / Wusyep Yihre dialect, the same variety as the 2018 SIL dictionary and the 1993 Acts translation 'Yehre Dialect'); glottocode urat1244 (language level; Glottolog lists no dialect sub-codes). They note dialect differences in segmentals (Urat I uses /k/ for glottal stop, has syllabic nasals) but say nothing about stress differing across dialects.

sources.note: Sec. 4.2 p.31: stress predictable and non-phonemic; ultimate if the final syllable is closed, penultimate if the final syllable is open ('apply to the majority of words'). Sec. 4.1: length and tone not pertinent at word level. Sec. 0.2 p.3: 'Since stress is predictable, it is not usually written.' Sec. 5.1 p.34: syllable defined as unit of potential stress placement. Vowel allophony (pp.27-28) conditioned by stressed vs unstressed syllables.
